verdicts.trueWording: no reviewer recognised Weer’s deathly state
verdicts.note: Live raw fetch of lareviewofbooks.org (HTTP 200) carries verbatim: 'as Wright points out, “no reviewer recognised Weer’s deathly state ... and the ghost’s story quickly became Wolfe’s first misinterpreted narrative.”' Wright's Attending Daedalus is named as the source two sentences earlier; Weer is identified as the novel's narrator. The live SPA HTML omits the byline, so the 'Joan Gordon' limb and the 30 April 2013 date were confirmed on the Wayback raw capture of the same URL ('We Read Things Differently By Joan Gordon APRIL 30, 2013'). 'When Peace first appeared' rests on 'no reviewer' + 'quickly became Wolfe's first misinterpreted narrative' plus the review's opening on the 1975 publication.

verdicts.trueWording: although I vehemently disagree that Wolfe’s goal is to confound
verdicts.note: Verbatim on the live raw page: 'I have to admit that the ghost story is probably the correct interpretation, although I vehemently disagree that Wolfe’s goal is to confound the reader.' The confounding claim is attributed to Wright in the preceding sentence ('as Wright says later ... “This element of choice is Wolfe’s principal device for confounding the reader.”'). Byline Joan Gordon confirmed on the Wayback capture of the same URL.

verdicts.trueWording: but the novel merely notes that she has grown
verdicts.note: Verbatim: 'Borski describes Olivia as “overeating — a classic symptom of rejection,” but the novel merely notes that she has grown “plump ... until she was a comfortable size 14,” as a result of not having to cook for herself any longer.' The elaborate symbolic reading limb is supported by the surrounding paragraph (Borski's 'Brimstone Trail', 'Alden Dennis Weer may be the Devil incarnate', Olivia 'embodying the fire-and-brimstone connection'). Byline Joan Gordon confirmed on the Wayback capture.

verdicts.trueWording: designed to ‘convey the flavour of an odd place at an odd time.’
verdicts.note: Live raw fetch of ultan.org.uk/review-botns/ (HTTP 200), 'Mapping a Masterwork', 28 August 2002, 'Reviewed by Peter Wright'. Page: 'Wolfe elaborates his textual games-playing by introducing significant levels unfamiliar diction, designed to ‘convey the flavour of an odd place at an odd time.’ 8'. Footnote 8 on the same page reads 'Gene Wolfe, Castle of Days (New York: Tor, 1992) p. 236', so the words are Wolfe's, quoted by Wright, about the unfamiliar diction.

verdicts.trueWording: obscure nouns ... ‘intended to be suggestive rather than definitive’
verdicts.note: Page: 'In his appendix to The Shadow of the Torturer, Wolfe invests his diction with an enforced polysemy when he explains that the obscure nouns found in his ‘translation’ of The Book of the New Sun are “intended to be suggestive rather than definitive”. 9' Footnote 9 = 'Gene Wolfe, The Shadow of the Torturer (London: Arrow, 1981), p. 302'. Every limb (Wolfe, appendix, obscure nouns, quoted by Wright) is on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: unreliable because of the very characteristic that makes him appear wholly reliable
verdicts.note: Verbatim on the page: 'Ironically, Severian is unreliable because of the very characteristic that makes him appear wholly reliable: his eidetic memory.' Author Peter Wright named in the page's byline block ('Reviewed by Peter Wright').

verdicts.trueWording: mnemonists ... remember a wealth of detail (plot) which scatters meaning (story)
verdicts.note: Verbatim: 'given that mnemonists have a tendency to remember a wealth of detail (plot) which scatters meaning (story)'. The narrator limb is supported in the adjoining sentences ('it is his status as a mnemonist that marks Severian as someone who cannot be trusted'). Wright's parenthetical equates the scattered meaning with the story, as the claim renders it.

verdicts.trueWording: alerts the reader ... a complex and contrived textual game
verdicts.note: Verbatim: 'The gulf between plot and story, between the apparent and the real, alerts the reader to the fact that Wolfe is playing a complex and contrived textual game that facilitates a number of methods of interpretation.'

verdicts.trueWording: by effectively concealing his narratological sleight of hand
verdicts.note: Verbatim: 'Rather, by effectively concealing his narratological sleight of hand and constructing a puzzle for his reader, Wolfe attempts to alert that reader to the level of perception required.' The 'rather than displaying it' limb is carried by the contrast Wright sets up immediately before ('He is not necessarily preoccupied with demonstrating how proficient he is as a writer. Rather, ...') and after ('does not invite the reader to marvel at how clever Wolfe can be').

Verbatim: 'critics have tended to extol The Book of the New Sun for its fluidity of style, the conception of its enigmatic, alien Earth, and the depth of its characterisation. This conventional, narrow and unimaginative approach was unsatisfactory in 1983 and will remain so until readers take up the gauntlet Wolfe throws at their feet.' Both limbs present.

verdicts.trueWording: purposeful in establishing, within the first pages, Severian as an unreliable narrator
verdicts.note: Live lists.urth.net is dead (curl exit 28, HTTP 000); recovered via the Wayback raw capture 20210416053637id_ of the same URL, whose 'link: rel="original"' header matches. Message is by 'b sharp', Wed Sep 6 05:48:33 PDT 2006. Verbatim: 'they were Sev’s mistakes not Wolfe’s, and that they are purposeful in establishing, within the first pages, Severian as an unreliable narrator.' The rejection limb is explicit ('I can’t see a repeat of a mistake in an appendix as proof positive of auctorial error') against the quoted claim 'so the mistake is probably Wolfe’s'. The message page names the interlocutor only as 'Roy'; the surname Lackey was confirmed off-page from the archive's September 2006 author index (Roy C. Lackey posted five messages in this same 'Close Reading: Torturer Chapter I' thread).
